For day thirteen of the spring sale there are a ton of new sales. I'm not going to cover all the games on sale, since they have a ton, but I'll pick some that I feel strongly about from each day.

Fight The Dragon
Obviously this game is meant to be a player-driven experience, because there is very little developer-designed content. Luckily the players have actually made a ton of good maps, so there's plenty to do - and this game is fun co-op.

The final dragon level is actually meant as a sort of score board - so you can only face him solo and he'll probably slaughter you. You get a reward based on how much damage you did though, you don't have to kill him in one shot.

 

Never Alone
A little platformer with a cute style, but flawed gameplay that can be frustrating at times. Most of the interesting bonus material about the Alaskan people is told through videos that you can watch between levels - which I didn't mind but some people might not like.

 

Proteus
There isn't much to this game - maybe an hour of walking around in a world where everything makes different sounds. The visual style is very cool and would be a nice addition to Minecraft, but there isn't really anything to do here. I usually don't mind walking simulator games, but this one bored me while i was waiting for the seasons to change.

 

Contagion
This is primarily a multiplayer game - although you could play a few of the scenario maps solo. These maps are actually my biggest complaint about the multiplayer, because you'll probably be dropping in after the game starts - unless you're playing with friends. When this happens it's pretty hard to find other people, or the objectives, unless you're already very familiar with the maps.

There's also a Last Man Standing mode where dead people become zombies and hunt the living players, and I actually liked hunting better than trying to win. Interesting experience.

 

Reus
You control multiple gods, transforming the environment of a barren planet to help tribes of people flourish. The core of the gameplay is growth objectives for the tribes, which eventually unlock more abilities for your gods. A lot of this revolves around making different combinations of plants, animals, and minerals in the world for the villagers to use.

It's a bit of world building with a slight puzzle feel to it, and I really enjoyed it the first time through. I don't feel like it has a ton of replayability though.

 

Little Inferno
Do you like to burn things? Because that's basically all you do in this game, it's a fireplace simulator. You burn gifts that are delivered in the mail (actually quite satisfying - they all feel different), and then use coins from that to buy more items out of a catalogue. The main game mechanic is a combo system where you have to figure out which items to burn together to get achievements.

There is a tiny bit of a story overarching the whole thing too, and that was rather cute.

 

Red Faction Collection
I've only played Red Faction 1 and Armageddon, but the whole series is really known for how destructable the environments are in the games. The first one is quite old and pretty innovative in that respect, you can tunnel through most of the rock in the game using your weapons.

Armageddon prevents terrain destruction but even massive buildings can be knocked down, and it's pretty cool to see - although the camera is a tight-third person view like console games. That makes it a bit more annoying than it should be.

The enemies in this game are pretty easy, and in many places you can just run past them until you hit one of the numerous cutscenes (which despawns everything chasing you). Weapons are also limited, 4 slots. It's very obviously a console experience, and has a lot of strange design decisions that seem more like they were focused on the technical aspects of the game instead of making sure it was fun.

 

Hero Siege
This is one of the few games I've reviewed where I feel like my video doesn't completely represent the current state of the game. I went back and played it again a few months ago, and the balance was completely different than when I reviewed it.

Originally I thought the balance was strange, since items you get during the levels have a huge impact on your stats - so you can't really start on a high level since you lose all your items on death. They apparently changed this, but don't seem to have buffed the actual character stats, which makes it feel pretty slow - even on the same characters that I had put a few hours into leveling up before.

This is a shame because I like the mechanics of the classes in this shoot-em-up, but now the enemies don't explode fast enough to make it feel exciting and satisfying.

 

Walking Dead
Obviously this series is known for having a good story - it's basically a choose your own adventure game with point-and-click elements. The downside is that a lot of your choices have no real relevance to the story - often they just choose which of your companions is present during the journey, not what actually happens.

This lack of actual choice was a bit disappointing, but the story is still interesting - so if linearity doesn't bother you it may still be worth a look.

 

McPixel
This game is incredibly shallow, you only have a few seconds to defuse a bomb on each level - and if you get it wrong you instantly go on to the next one, looping back to the one you failed eventually.

It wouldn't have quite the same chaotic feel, but I wish you could finish one level before moving on - because there's no real indication of the right answer. At least that way you could feel like you solved it, rather than finally got it right by accident.

 

Botanicula
The atmosphere and art style of this little point-and-click are pretty great - but it is shallow. A lot of hunting around different screens, not puzzle solving like their previous game Machinarium.

 

Darksiders
The world in this hack-n-slash is pretty cool, and the weapons are satisfying. It is quite linear, but they designed it well enough that it doesn't feel like a corridor - and I actually got a good Legend Of Zelda vibe from it. If you like those type of games this series might be worth a look.

 

Home
This one has a low resolution and rough pixel-art graphics, and is pretty short too - about an hour per playthrough. To see the other endings you have to replay the entire thing, which is weird since the actual gameplay doesn't seem to be very relevant to the story at the end - it's generated based on choices you make at the end of the game. Strange.

 

Splice
A puzzle game that's all about splicing cells together in the correct order to rearrange an organism to match the blueprint shown. You have to delete, move, and grow cells in a limited number of moves - and there's usually one right answer on the order of operations to do this. It can be pretty tricky. I wasn't thrilled by this game, but it wasn't bad - though I think it could use a good hint system.

Q: Do you know who loves mulch? A: Worms. Q: Do you know who loves worm shit? A: Your Plants!

Get down to your local compost today and get some free garden mulch! Grass clippings and leaves are excelent garden mulch.

Hey @earthgleaner, we built two 5x6 foot bins to start composting the tremendous amounts of garden waste that I trim off each season from my perennial gardens and will soon be adding our kitchen peelings to the pile (we just need to add doors to the front of the bins to keep things tidy). Any advice as to what I can do to get that beautiful compost started? Right now, it just seems to sit there.

The rule of thumb is 2 parts brown to 1 part green. Browns are: dried leaves , srheded newspaper, old hay or straw. Lawn clippings are kinda in-between brown and green. Greens are: bananna peels, apple cores, melon rinds, and any other rich sources of nutrients. Turning it from time to time helps. Make sure to cover you "greens" with your "browns" and try to layer it like this as you go. Covering up the bananna peels and such will make it food for the worms instead of the flies. If you layer like this you shouldn't have to turn the pile as much.

You can add red wigglers if you want. I'm in a cold climate so I have a worm bin indoors. In the late spring I harvest the worm castings and put some of the worms in my compost pile outside. You don't have to buy a bunch of worms if you can find a friend wo has some. Or just give it some time for nature to take its course.

Compost is like slow burning fire. You need to give it some time for all the critters to settle in before you really get to see more movement.

Thank you so much! I have read about green and brown layers but it was always presented in a very complicated manner. This seems very straight forward.

A couple of quick questions....any weeds pulled or green trimmings from plants would be green, correct? And if some dirt ends up in there (ie bits of green sod with earth when I edge my beds, or on the roots of pulled plants), will that matter?

I hope to get the layers started soon. Having the two bins will help me organise the pile that's already there.

Yes and Yes.

The awesome thing about composting is that nature is very forgiving. Science can help but if you just throw everyting onto a pile, it will more or less correct itself.

Everything EarthGleaner mentioned is great, I just have one thing to add. I live in a very dry climate, and I actually had to water my compost to get it started, otherwise it tended to just sit there and desiccate. If the pile has enough mass, it doesn't take more than a few good drenchings to get the ball rolling. Covering it with a tarp or something help to keep it from drying out. General Guide:

Early Game: Focus on eating blobs and avoid other blobs. Viruses (green spiky things) can hide you under them. Also stay away from corners since it's easy to get trapped there.

Mid Game: Once you're fairly larger than viruses, try to eat other players by forcing them into corners/walls or splitting (Space Bar). Careful with splitting, because if you aren't more than double your prey's size they'll eat you instead :(

Late Game/Leaderboard: Splitting is crucial at this point, as well as extremely risky. It is a terrible idea to split when facing another leaderboarder, but splitting to eat medium-sized blobs is a good way to grow quickly. However, splitting puts you at a huge disadvantage until you reform, because another leaderboarder can just eat you.
Try to watch other leaderboarders to see when they split. to eat someone else, and then eat their smaller blobs without splitting.

Useful Strategies:

Escape:

Wall-hugging: Moving your mouse past the invisible boundary will cause your blob to squish up against the wall, reducing its size by a considerable amount (about 1/3). This is very useful for escapes since it's much harder to eat a small blob.

W-spamming: If you are trying to run away from someone who can eat you because you're about to be trapped, spam W through the opening. This will cause you to become smaller and faster, allowing you to get through the gap. The best part is, you only lose 10% mass since you'll just pick the mass back up!

Attack:

Virus-shooting: Shoot mass at Viruses with w and they'll grow in size. When they reach a certain size they split another virus off in whichever direction you were shooting your mass. This splits up the bigger blobs into bite sized pieces. (Thanks to u/dis_is_my_account)
